Filing Eligibility Calculator

Enter your prior case details to calculate your earliest eligible filing and discharge dates.

Home›Filing Bankruptcy Again›Filing Eligibility Calculator

Enter the filing date and chapter of your prior case, how it ended, and the chapter you want to file now. The calculator checks all applicable discharge bars, filing bars, and stay limits.

Eligibility Calculator

Full interactive calculator: Use the comprehensive free screener at 1328f.com/check.html - it checks all Section 1328(f), 727(a)(8), 727(a)(9), and 109(g) bars automatically.

To check your eligibility manually, you need:

Filing date of your prior case

Chapter filed (7, 13, 11, or 12)

How it ended (discharged, dismissed, or converted)

Date of discharge (if applicable)

Chapter you want to file now

Quick Reference

PriorNewWaitEarliest New Filing

Ch.7 (discharged)Ch.78 yearsPrior filing date + 8 years

Ch.7 (discharged)Ch.134 yearsPrior filing date + 4 years

Ch.13 (discharged)Ch.76 years*Prior filing date + 6 years*

Ch.13 (discharged)Ch.132 yearsPrior filing date + 2 years

Any (dismissed)Any0-180 daysDepends on 109(g)

* Exception if Ch.13 paid 100% or 70%+ in good faith with best effort

Step-by-Step Manual Check

Check 109(g): Was your prior case dismissed for willful failure to obey court orders, or voluntarily after a stay relief motion? If yes, you cannot file for 180 days from dismissal. 109g.org calculator

Check discharge bars: Was a discharge entered? If yes, look up the applicable bar from the chart above. 1328f.com screener

Check stay limits: Was a case dismissed within the past year? If yes, the stay will be limited (362(c)(3)) or absent (362(c)(4)). automaticstay.org

If no bars apply: You can file and receive a discharge immediately (subject to completing all requirements of the new case).

## Dismissed vs Discharged Bankruptcy [2026]: How Each Outcome Affects Refiling Eligibility
Source: https://canifileagain.org/dismissed-vs-discharged.html

Skip to main content

canifileagain.org
☰

Home
Waiting Periods
Dismissed vs Discharged
Calculator
State Rules
Strategic Refiling

Dismissed vs. Discharged - Impact on Refiling

Understanding the difference between dismissed and discharged cases is essential for refiling strategy.

Home›Filing Bankruptcy Again›Dismissed vs. Discharged - Impact on Refiling

Discharged means debts were eliminated - a successful outcome. Dismissed means the case was terminated without eliminating any debts. The distinction determines which refiling rules apply.

Discharged - Successful Outcome

A discharge eliminates your personal liability for covered debts. It is the goal of filing bankruptcy.

Consequences for refiling:

Discharge bars apply - You must wait the required period before receiving another discharge

No stay limits - The automatic stay is not limited by a prior discharge (only by prior dismissals)

Can file anytime - You can file a new case at any time for the automatic stay, but cannot receive a discharge until the bar period expires

Dismissed - Case Terminated, Debts Remain

A dismissal ends the case without eliminating debts. All obligations remain fully enforceable.

Consequences for refiling:

No discharge bar - Since no discharge was received, discharge bars do not apply

109(g) may apply - If dismissed for willful failure to obey court orders or after a stay relief motion

Stay limits apply - 362(c)(3): stay limited to 30 days if one dismissal within past year. 362(c)(4): no stay at all if two+ dismissals within past year

The stay limits are the biggest risk. A dismissed case does not create a discharge bar, but it can severely limit or eliminate the automatic stay in your next filing.

Common Reasons for Dismissal

Failure to file required documents within 14 days

Failure to complete credit counseling before filing

Failure to make Chapter 13 plan payments

Failure to appear at the 341 meeting

Failure to pass the means test (Chapter 7)

Voluntary dismissal by the debtor

Strategic Considerations

If you are deciding whether to request dismissal or let your case continue:

Dismissal preserves discharge eligibility in a future case (no bar is triggered)

But dismissal creates stay risks for future filings within one year

Conversion may be better - converting from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 (or vice versa) keeps the case open and avoids the stay limits

See also: Strategic refiling | All waiting periods

## Can I File Bankruptcy Again? - Waiting Periods [2026]
Source: https://canifileagain.org/

🌐 Esta página está disponible en Español

Part of the Open Bankruptcy Project - 210+ free domains, 49,000+ pages, $0 hosting

Can I File Bankruptcy Again?

Plain English guide to every waiting period, filing bar, and stay limit that affects repeat bankruptcy filers.

Quick Answer

Yes, you can file bankruptcy again, but waiting periods apply. Chapter 7 after Chapter 7: 8 years. Chapter 13 after Chapter 7: 4 years. Chapter 13 after Chapter 13: 2 years. Chapter 7 after Chapter 13: 6 years. All periods run from filing date to filing date. See the complete timing chart.

Yes, but waiting periods apply. Ch.7-to-Ch.7: 8 years (727(a)(8)). Ch.7-to-Ch.13: 4 years (1328(f)(1)). Measured filing date to filing date.

Can You File Bankruptcy Again?

Yes - but when and how depends on your prior case. The Bankruptcy Code imposes different waiting periods depending on which chapter you filed, which chapter you want to file now, and how your prior case ended. If you need to start the process, see our step-by-step filing guide. Repeat filers should also consider tax debt in repeat filings, as unpaid taxes may survive discharge.

Discharge Bars - Waiting Periods

Prior CaseNew CaseWaitStatute

Chapter 7Chapter 78 years727(a)(8)

Chapter 7Chapter 134 years1328(f)(1)

Chapter 13Chapter 76 years*727(a)(9)

Chapter 13Chapter 132 years1328(f)(2)

* Exception if prior Ch.13 paid 100% or 70%+ in good faith with best effort.

Key: Measured from filing date to filing date. Prior discharge must have been received.

Filing Bars

Section 109(g) - 180-Day Bar

Applies if prior case dismissed for willful failure to obey court orders, or voluntarily dismissed after a stay relief motion. The dismissal rate by district varies widely and may affect how courts view your refiling.

Full guide at 109g.org →

Automatic Stay Limits

362(c)(3) - One Prior Dismissal

The automatic stay protection in bankruptcy terminates after 30 days unless court extends it.

362(c)(4) - Two+ Prior Dismissals

No stay takes effect without court order.

## State Refiling Rules [2026]: Exemption-Domicile Lookback, Venue, and Local Court Practice
Source: https://canifileagain.org/state-rules.html

Skip to main content

canifileagain.org
☰

Home
Waiting Periods
Dismissed vs Discharged
Calculator
State Rules
Strategic Refiling

State Rules for Refiling Bankruptcy

Federal discharge bars are the same everywhere, but state exemption rules may affect your refiling strategy.

Home›Filing Bankruptcy Again›State Rules for Refiling Bankruptcy

The waiting periods (discharge bars) are federal and apply uniformly nationwide. But state exemption laws, the 2-year domicile rule, and the homestead cap may affect the strategic timing of your filing.

Federal Rules Are Uniform

The discharge bars - 727(a)(8), 727(a)(9), 1328(f)(1), 1328(f)(2) - are federal law and apply the same in every state. The 180-day filing bar under 109(g) is also federal. No state can change these waiting periods.

However, state law affects other aspects of your bankruptcy that may influence when and how to file again.

State Exemption Impact

Exemptions determine what property you can keep in bankruptcy. They vary dramatically by state:

Homestead: Texas and Florida offer unlimited homestead exemptions. Many states cap the exemption at $25,000 to $250,000.

Vehicles: Ranges from $1,000 (some states) to $15,000+ (others)

Wildcard: Some states offer a "wildcard" exemption that can be applied to any property

Federal vs. state: Some states allow you to choose between federal exemptions and state exemptions. Others require you to use state exemptions.

Strategic timing: If you recently moved from a state with generous exemptions to one with more limited exemptions, it may be worth waiting until the 2-year domicile period expires to use your new state's exemptions (or vice versa).

The 2-Year Domicile Rule

Section 522(b)(3)(A) requires you to use the exemption laws of the state where you have been domiciled for the 730 days (2 years) before filing.

If you have not been in your current state for 2 years, you must use the exemptions of the state where you were domiciled for the 180-day period before that 730-day period. This can create complicated situations for recent movers.

The Homestead Cap for Recent Movers

Section 522(p) caps the homestead exemption at $214,000 (adjusted periodically) if the debtor acquired the homestead within the 1,215 days (approximately 3.3 years) before filing and cannot trace the equity to a prior home in the same state.

This prevents "exemption planning" - buying an expensive home in a state with unlimited homestead exemption shortly before filing bankruptcy.

Related: Strategic refiling considerations | All waiting periods

## Automatic Stay Limits for Repeat Filers
Source: https://canifileagain.org/stay-limits.html

canifileagain.org

1328f.com1328f.org

Can I File Bankruptcy Again?

Free tool to check if you can file bankruptcy again. Discharge bars, waiting periods, and prior filing restrictions explained.

Home›Filing Bankruptcy Again›Can I File Bankruptcy Again?

The automatic stay is a court order that takes effect immediately when you file bankruptcy. It stops most collection actions, lawsuits, foreclosures, repossessions, wage garnishments, and creditor harassment. It remains in effect until the case is closed or the debt is discharged.

One Prior Dismissal - 30-Day Stay

Section 362(c)(3): If you had a case pending and dismissed within the year before your new filing, the automatic stay expires after 30 days unless you file a motion to extend it. You must show the new filing is in good faith.

Two or More Prior Dismissals - No Stay

Section 362(c)(4): If you had two or more cases pending and dismissed within the year before filing, you get NO automatic stay at all. You must file a motion and prove good faith to get any stay protection. Until the court grants your motion, creditors can continue collection.

How to Extend the Stay

File a motion to extend or impose the stay before it expires (within 30 days for 362(c)(3), or as soon as possible for 362(c)(4)). Demonstrate that the new case is filed in good faith - changed circumstances, ability to complete the plan, specific reason prior case was dismissed. Full serial filing guide.

## Strategic Bankruptcy Refiling [2026]: Chapter 20, Plan Conversion, and Lien Stripping Timing
Source: https://canifileagain.org/strategic-refiling.html

Skip to main content

canifileagain.org
☰

Home
Waiting Periods
Dismissed vs Discharged
Calculator
State Rules
Strategic Refiling

Strategic Refiling - When It Makes Sense

Refiling bankruptcy is not always a sign of failure. Changed circumstances, a different chapter, or strategic timing can make a new filing the right choice.

Home›Filing Bankruptcy Again›Strategic Refiling - When It Makes Sense

When circumstances have genuinely changed: new debts accumulated since discharge, change in income or employment, medical emergency, divorce, or when a different chapter better suits your current situation.

Changed Circumstances

Life does not stop after a bankruptcy discharge. Legitimate reasons to refile include:

New debts - Medical bills, job loss, business failure after prior discharge

Income changes - Reduced income may now qualify you for Chapter 7 when you previously had to file Chapter 13

Divorce - Separation of finances may create new debt obligations

Foreclosure or repossession threat - Need the automatic stay to protect property

Lawsuit or judgment - New creditor actions require protection

Chapter Switching Strategy

Chapter 13 After Chapter 7

Common when the debtor needs to address secured debts (mortgages, car loans) that survived the Chapter 7 discharge. Chapter 13 can cure mortgage arrears, restructure car loans through cramdown, and address tax debts through the plan.

Chapter 7 After Chapter 13 Dismissal

If your Chapter 13 plan failed, Chapter 7 may provide faster relief - if you qualify under the means test. No discharge bar applies because the prior case was dismissed, not discharged.

Key advantage: If your prior case was dismissed (not discharged), there is no discharge bar for the new case. You can receive a discharge immediately.

Conversion vs. Dismissal and Refiling

If you are currently in a bankruptcy case, converting to a different chapter is often better than dismissing and refiling:

OptionProsCons

Convert (e.g., Ch.13 to Ch.7)No stay limits, preserves filing date, no gap in protectionMay not qualify for conversion, means test applies

Dismiss and refileClean slate, choose any chapterStay may be limited (362(c)(3)/(c)(4)), gap in protection

Timing Your Refiling

Strategic timing considerations:

Wait for the discharge bar to expire if you need a discharge (not just the automatic stay)

Wait 1+ years after dismissal to avoid stay limits under 362(c)(3)/(c)(4)

Wait for domicile requirements if you recently moved and want to use your new state's exemptions

File before foreclosure sale if you need the stay to save your home

File before garnishment starts if a judgment has been entered but garnishment has not begun

Use the screener: 1328f.com discharge screener | Filing calculator

## Bankruptcy Waiting Periods [2026]: 8/6/4/2 Year Rule Under 727(a)(8) and 1328(f)
Source: https://canifileagain.org/waiting-periods.html

Skip to main content

canifileagain.org
☰

Home
Waiting Periods
Dismissed vs Discharged
Calculator
State Rules
Strategic Refiling

Bankruptcy Waiting Periods - Complete Chart

Every waiting period that affects repeat filers. Filing bars, discharge bars, and automatic stay limits.

Home›Filing Bankruptcy Again›Bankruptcy Waiting Periods - Complete Chart

Ch.7 to Ch.7: 8 years. Ch.7 to Ch.13: 4 years. Ch.13 to Ch.7: 6 years (with exceptions). Ch.13 to Ch.13: 2 years. All measured filing date to filing date.

Discharge Bars - Master Chart

Prior CaseNew CaseWaiting PeriodStatute

Chapter 7Chapter 78 years727(a)(8)

Chapter 7Chapter 134 years1328(f)(1)

Chapter 13Chapter 76 years*727(a)(9)

Chapter 13Chapter 132 years1328(f)(2)

Chapter 12Chapter 76 years*727(a)(9)

Chapter 11Chapter 7None (disputed)727(a)(8) - "under this chapter"

* The 6-year bar does not apply if the prior Ch.13 paid unsecured creditors 100%, or paid at least 70% and the plan was proposed in good faith with best effort.

Key rule: All bars are measured from filing date to filing date. The prior case must have resulted in a discharge. A dismissed case does not trigger discharge bars (but may trigger 109(g)).

Filing Bars

Section 109(g) - 180-Day Bar

You cannot file at all for 180 days if:

Your prior case was dismissed for willful failure to abide by orders of the court or to appear before the court

You voluntarily dismissed your prior case after a creditor filed a motion for relief from stay

The 109(g) bar prevents filing, not just discharge. You cannot even get the automatic stay during the 180-day period.

Full guide: 109g.org

Automatic Stay Limits for Repeat Filers

Section 362(c)(3) - One Prior Dismissal in Past Year

If you had one case pending and dismissed within the past year, the automatic stay in your new case automatically terminates after 30 days unless the court extends it.

To extend: file a motion before the 30 days expire. You must show the new filing is in good faith.

Section 362(c)(4) - Two+ Prior Dismissals in Past Year

If you had two or more cases pending and dismissed within the past year, no automatic stay takes effect at all unless the court orders it.

To get the stay: file an emergency motion. You must show changed circumstances and good faith.

This is the harshest penalty for repeat filings. Without the automatic stay, creditors can continue foreclosure, repossession, garnishment, and all other collection actions even though a bankruptcy is pending.

Check Your Dates

Use these free tools to calculate your earliest eligible filing and discharge dates:

1328f.com discharge screener - Checks all Section 1328(f) and 727(a)(8)/(9) bars

109g.org calculator - 180-day filing bar calculator

727a8.com - 8-year Chapter 7 discharge bar

See also: Dismissed vs. discharged - what it means for refiling

## Privacy Policy - canifileagain.org
Source: https://canifileagain.org/privacy.html

canifileagain.org

Home
Privacy

Privacy Policy

How we handle your data. Short version: we don't sell it, share it, or use it for advertising.

Data We Collect

We use Google Analytics (GA4) to measure aggregate site traffic. This includes page views, session duration, approximate geographic region (country and city level), and device type. We do not collect names, email addresses, or personally identifiable information through analytics.

Aggregate event data from Google Analytics is also exported to Google BigQuery for research use. The BigQuery data is used only for internal trajectory analysis and network health reports, is not shared with third parties, and is not used for advertising.

What We Don't Do

We do not sell data. We do not run advertising. We do not collect financial information. We do not use retargeting. We do not share any user data with attorneys, law firms, creditors, debt collectors, or legal service providers.

Specifically, we do not enable Google Signals, Google Ads integration, User-ID collection, or any cross-device tracking feature in Google Analytics. GA4 operates in aggregate-traffic-measurement mode only on this site.

Cookies

We use only first-party cookies set by Google Analytics for aggregate traffic measurement. We do not use advertising cookies, tracking pixels, or third-party analytics cookies.

Third-Party Services

Google Analytics (GA4) - aggregate traffic measurement

Google BigQuery - aggregate event data warehouse for research use only; not shared, not used for advertising

Google Search Console - search query measurement (clicks, impressions, our own page rankings)

GitHub Pages - hosting

Contact Forms & Email

This site may link to contact forms or email addresses operated by the Open Bankruptcy Project. Any data you submit through those channels is handled under the Open Bankruptcy Project master privacy policy, which governs all sites in this network.

Children's Privacy

This site is not directed at children under 13. We do not knowingly collect information from children.

Data Retention

Analytics data is retained for 14 months per Google's standard retention settings. After that window, individual event data is automatically deleted by Google; aggregate report metrics remain available.

Your Rights

You may request deletion of any personal data we hold by contacting info@openbankruptcyproject.org. California residents have additional rights under CCPA. EU residents have additional rights under GDPR. All such requests are handled by the Open Bankruptcy Project.

Network Policy

This site is part of the Open Bankruptcy Project operated by the Open Bankruptcy Project, a 501(c)(3) public charity (EIN 41-5159631). The same privacy standards apply across every site in the network. The authoritative master policy is maintained at https://openbankruptcyproject.org/privacy.html.

Changes

We may update this policy from time to time. Changes are reflected on the master policy first and then mirrored across all network sites. Check the master policy for the most current version.

Effective: March 30, 2026  |  Updated: April 11, 2026

Home  ·  Privacy  ·  Open Bankruptcy Project

Part of the Open Bankruptcy Project. Educational information only - not legal advice.

No ads. No affiliate links. No data sold. Supported by donations.

## About canifileagain.org
Source: https://canifileagain.org/about.html

canifileagain.org

Home
About
Privacy

About canifileagain.org

Part of the Open Bankruptcy Project operated by the Open Bankruptcy Project.

What This Site Is

canifileagain.org is an educational resource operated by the Open Bankruptcy Project, a 501(c)(3) public charity (EIN 41-5159631). It's part of the Open Bankruptcy Project - a collection of free, public-interest sites that translate federal bankruptcy court data, statutes, and procedures into language ordinary people can use.

The Open Bankruptcy Project

The Open Bankruptcy Project builds free, open-source tools that make public bankruptcy court data accessible to the people it affects most - debtors, advocates, researchers, journalists, and policymakers. Every screening tool, analysis script, and dataset is published on GitHub. Anyone can audit, reproduce, or build upon the work without permission or payment.

Our research is derived primarily from the Federal Judicial Center's Integrated Database covering all federal bankruptcy filings 2008 through 2024, cross-referenced with PACER docket data via the Free Law Project's RECAP archive and independent court-scraping tooling. Methodology and source code are public.

What This Site Is Not

This site is not a law firm. We do not represent clients, file bankruptcy cases, or give legal advice. We do not receive referral fees, affiliate commissions, or advertising revenue. We do not sell data.

If you need legal advice about your specific situation, consult a licensed bankruptcy attorney in your state.

Research Contributions

Our research supports two accepted suggestions to the Federal Judicial Conference Advisory Committee on Bankruptcy Rules:

Suggestion 26-BK-3 - procedural screening for 11 U.S.C. § 1328(f) re-filing eligibility

Suggestion 26-BK-5 - Rule 9037 / Form 121 / Form 309E1 amendments addressing systematic unredacted Social Security number exposure on federal bankruptcy dockets

Contact

General inquiries, data requests, research collaboration, and media: info@openbankruptcyproject.org

Privacy and Data Handling

See our privacy policy for details. Short version: aggregate analytics only; no data sold, no advertising, no attorney referrals, no financial information collected.

Home  ·  About  ·  Privacy  ·  Open Bankruptcy Project

Part of the Open Bankruptcy Project. Educational information only - not legal advice.

No ads. No affiliate links. No data sold. Supported by donations.

## Can I File Bankruptcy Again in Alabama? [2026] Refile Timing Rules
Source: https://canifileagain.org/states/alabama.html

← canifileagain.org home

Can I File Bankruptcy Again in Alabama? [2026] Refile Timing Rules

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Alabama residents.

Can You File Bankruptcy Again in Alabama?

Yes - but the timing depends on three separate federal statutes and the reason your prior case ended. This page walks through each bar for Alabama filers.

Section 727(a)(8) - 8-year bar on a second Chapter 7 discharge after a prior Chapter 7 discharge.

Section 1328(f) - 4-year bar on a Chapter 13 discharge when the prior case was a Chapter 7/11/12 discharge (measured from the filing date of the prior case, not the discharge date).

Section 109(g) - 180-day bar on any new filing when the prior case was dismissed for willful failure to abide by court orders or was voluntarily dismissed after a motion for relief from stay.

Alabama bankruptcy courts apply 109(g) strictly. Dismissed-with-prejudice orders typically specify a 180-day or 1-year bar; some include a 2-year bar for serial filers.

Section 727(a)(8): The 8-Year Chapter 7-After-Chapter 7 Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 727(a)(8), a Chapter 7 debtor cannot receive a second Chapter 7 discharge within 8 years of filing the prior case that produced a discharge.

The 8 years runs from filing date to filing date, not discharge to filing.

If the prior case was dismissed rather than discharged, 727(a)(8) does not bar the refile - but 109(g) might.

A Alabama filer whose prior Chapter 7 was filed January 1, 2018, can file a new Chapter 7 on or after January 1, 2026.

See the 727(a)(8) eight-year rule for the full mechanics.

Section 1328(f): The 4-Year Chapter 13-After-Chapter 7 Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 1328(f)(1), a Chapter 13 debtor cannot receive a discharge if a Chapter 7, 11, or 12 discharge was entered in a case filed within 4 years before the current filing.

This is the so-called "Chapter 20" strategy: filing Chapter 7 first for unsecured-debt discharge, then Chapter 13 to cram down or cure secured debt. The Chapter 13 can still be filed before the 4 years, but without a discharge at completion.

Section 1328(f)(2) adds a 2-year bar on Chapter 13 after a prior Chapter 13 discharge.

4 years is from filing date of prior case to filing date of new case, not discharge date.

For Alabama filers considering the Chapter 20 route, the 4-year bar is a planning constraint, not an absolute stopper - many debtors file the second case intentionally knowing a no-discharge plan still works.

See the 1328(f) four-year rule for a worked example.

Section 109(g): The 180-Day Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 109(g), a debtor cannot be a debtor in any chapter for 180 days after a prior case is dismissed if either:

109(g)(1) - the case was dismissed for "willful failure" to abide by court orders or to appear in proper prosecution of the case; or

109(g)(2) - the debtor voluntarily dismissed the case after a creditor filed a motion for relief from the automatic stay (MFRS).

AL chapter 13 dismissal rates are historically high, so 109(g) is a live issue.

109(g)(2) is the most common trap for Alabama vehicle-loan and mortgage debtors: after a creditor files MFRS, if the debtor voluntarily dismisses to avoid an adverse ruling, the 180-day bar kicks in automatically - no court order needed.

See 109(g) dismissal bar.

Dismissal With Prejudice in Alabama

Separate from the statutory 180 days, Alabama bankruptcy courts can dismiss a case "with prejudice" under 11 U.S.C. Section 349(a) and bar refiling for a longer period - commonly 1 year, 2 years, or (rarely) permanently.

Typical triggers in Alabama practice:

Serial filings designed to stop foreclosure without any plan of reorganization.

Failure to make plan payments repeatedly across multiple cases.

Bad-faith filings where the petition was not accompanied by schedules or where schedules contained materially false statements.

Dismissal with prejudice orders bind the debtor under res judicata and must be vacated (via Rule 60(b)) before any refile.

Alabama Federal Bankruptcy Data

Refile timing in Alabama depends on both the federal statute and the local dismissal/relief-from-stay practices reflected in the case data.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,743 consumer bankruptcy cases from Alabama's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 7478n/an/a

Chapter 131,265n/an/a

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Stacking the Three Bars in Alabama

For a Alabama filer considering a second case, all three bars must be checked together:

Was the prior case discharged? If Chapter 7 discharged, 727(a)(8) controls (8 years Ch7 to Ch7; 1328(f) applies to Ch13 after Ch7 at 4 years). If Chapter 13 discharged, 1328(f)(2) bars another Ch13 discharge for 2 years.

Was the prior case dismissed? Check 109(g)(1) willful-failure ground and 109(g)(2) MFRS-voluntary-dismissal ground. Check the dismissal order for any "with prejudice" language.

Was there a sanctions order in the prior case? Some Alabama judges enter injunctions against refiling under 105(a) as part of sanctions, independent of 109(g) and 349.

Run our refile-timing calculator to see your earliest allowable refile date.

Alabama Chapter 20 Strategy

"Chapter 20" is the informal name for filing Chapter 7 to discharge unsecured debt, then filing Chapter 13 immediately after to restructure a mortgage, vehicle loan, or priority tax debt even though 1328(f) bars a second discharge.

In a Alabama Chapter 20, the second-case Chapter 13 plan:

Cures mortgage arrears under 1322(b)(5) over the plan term.

Strips wholly-unsecured junior mortgages where state valuation supports it.

Pays priority taxes and secured vehicle loans through the plan.

Does not result in a discharge at completion - but reorganization still proceeds.

For Alabama's high-dismissal chapter 13 environment, the Chapter 20 path often works better than a single Chapter 13 when substantial unsecured debt exists.

Corporate and Small-Business Refile Constraints

Note: entity debtors (LLCs, corporations) generally cannot file pro se - they must be represented by counsel to handle plan-level matters. This is a practical constraint on any refile strategy where the debtor is a business entity rather than an individual.

See corporate refile rules for the Sub V reorganization refile and the rules on pre-confirmation versus post-confirmation filings.

Related Alabama Resources

1328(f) four-year bar

109(g) 180-day bar

AK has one federal bankruptcy district covering the whole state.

Section 109(g): The 180-Day Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 109(g), a debtor cannot be a debtor in any chapter for 180 days after a prior case is dismissed if either:

109(g)(1) - the case was dismissed for "willful failure" to abide by court orders or to appear in proper prosecution of the case; or

109(g)(2) - the debtor voluntarily dismissed the case after a creditor filed a motion for relief from the automatic stay (MFRS).

AZ is a 9th Circuit jurisdiction; In re Leafty-style analysis controls.

109(g)(2) is the most common trap for Arizona vehicle-loan and mortgage debtors: after a creditor files MFRS, if the debtor voluntarily dismisses to avoid an adverse ruling, the 180-day bar kicks in automatically - no court order needed.

See 109(g) dismissal bar.

Dismissal With Prejudice in Arizona

Separate from the statutory 180 days, Arizona bankruptcy courts can dismiss a case "with prejudice" under 11 U.S.C. Section 349(a) and bar refiling for a longer period - commonly 1 year, 2 years, or (rarely) permanently.

Typical triggers in Arizona practice:

Serial filings designed to stop foreclosure without any plan of reorganization.

Failure to make plan payments repeatedly across multiple cases.

Bad-faith filings where the petition was not accompanied by schedules or where schedules contained materially false statements.

Dismissal with prejudice orders bind the debtor under res judicata and must be vacated (via Rule 60(b)) before any refile.

Stacking the Three Bars in Arizona

For a Arizona filer considering a second case, all three bars must be checked together:

Was the prior case discharged? If Chapter 7 discharged, 727(a)(8) controls (8 years Ch7 to Ch7; 1328(f) applies to Ch13 after Ch7 at 4 years). If Chapter 13 discharged, 1328(f)(2) bars another Ch13 discharge for 2 years.

Was the prior case dismissed? Check 109(g)(1) willful-failure ground and 109(g)(2) MFRS-voluntary-dismissal ground. Check the dismissal order for any "with prejudice" language.

Was there a sanctions order in the prior case? Some Arizona judges enter injunctions against refiling under 105(a) as part of sanctions, independent of 109(g) and 349.

Run our refile-timing calculator to see your earliest allowable refile date.

Arizona Chapter 20 Strategy

"Chapter 20" is the informal name for filing Chapter 7 to discharge unsecured debt, then filing Chapter 13 immediately after to restructure a mortgage, vehicle loan, or priority tax debt even though 1328(f) bars a second discharge.

In a Arizona Chapter 20, the second-case Chapter 13 plan:

Cures mortgage arrears under 1322(b)(5) over the plan term.

Strips wholly-unsecured junior mortgages where state valuation supports it.

Pays priority taxes and secured vehicle loans through the plan.

Does not result in a discharge at completion - but reorganization still proceeds.

For Arizona's high-dismissal chapter 13 environment, the Chapter 20 path often works better than a single Chapter 13 when substantial unsecured debt exists.

Corporate and Small-Business Refile Constraints

Note: entity debtors (LLCs, corporations) generally cannot file pro se - they must be represented by counsel to handle plan-level matters. This is a practical constraint on any refile strategy where the debtor is a business entity rather than an individual.

See corporate refile rules for the Sub V reorganization refile and the rules on pre-confirmation versus post-confirmation filings.

1328(f) four-year bar

109(g) 180-day bar

## Can I File Bankruptcy Again in Arkansas? [2026] Refile Timing Rules
Source: https://canifileagain.org/states/arkansas.html

← canifileagain.org home

Can I File Bankruptcy Again in Arkansas? [2026] Refile Timing Rules

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Arkansas residents.

Can You File Bankruptcy Again in Arkansas?

Yes - but the timing depends on three separate federal statutes and the reason your prior case ended. This page walks through each bar for Arkansas filers.

Section 727(a)(8) - 8-year bar on a second Chapter 7 discharge after a prior Chapter 7 discharge.

Section 1328(f) - 4-year bar on a Chapter 13 discharge when the prior case was a Chapter 7/11/12 discharge (measured from the filing date of the prior case, not the discharge date).

Section 109(g) - 180-day bar on any new filing when the prior case was dismissed for willful failure to abide by court orders or was voluntarily dismissed after a motion for relief from stay.

Arkansas bankruptcy courts frequently grant MFRS (motion for relief from stay) in vehicle and mortgage cases, which triggers 109(g)(2) if the debtor then voluntarily dismisses.

Section 727(a)(8): The 8-Year Chapter 7-After-Chapter 7 Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 727(a)(8), a Chapter 7 debtor cannot receive a second Chapter 7 discharge within 8 years of filing the prior case that produced a discharge.

The 8 years runs from filing date to filing date, not discharge to filing.

If the prior case was dismissed rather than discharged, 727(a)(8) does not bar the refile - but 109(g) might.

A Arkansas filer whose prior Chapter 7 was filed January 1, 2018, can file a new Chapter 7 on or after January 1, 2026.

See the 727(a)(8) eight-year rule for the full mechanics.

Section 1328(f): The 4-Year Chapter 13-After-Chapter 7 Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 1328(f)(1), a Chapter 13 debtor cannot receive a discharge if a Chapter 7, 11, or 12 discharge was entered in a case filed within 4 years before the current filing.

This is the so-called "Chapter 20" strategy: filing Chapter 7 first for unsecured-debt discharge, then Chapter 13 to cram down or cure secured debt. The Chapter 13 can still be filed before the 4 years, but without a discharge at completion.

Section 1328(f)(2) adds a 2-year bar on Chapter 13 after a prior Chapter 13 discharge.

4 years is from filing date of prior case to filing date of new case, not discharge date.

For Arkansas filers considering the Chapter 20 route, the 4-year bar is a planning constraint, not an absolute stopper - many debtors file the second case intentionally knowing a no-discharge plan still works.

See the 1328(f) four-year rule for a worked example.

Section 109(g): The 180-Day Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 109(g), a debtor cannot be a debtor in any chapter for 180 days after a prior case is dismissed if either:

109(g)(1) - the case was dismissed for "willful failure" to abide by court orders or to appear in proper prosecution of the case; or

109(g)(2) - the debtor voluntarily dismissed the case after a creditor filed a motion for relief from the automatic stay (MFRS).

8th Circuit authority applies.

109(g)(2) is the most common trap for Arkansas vehicle-loan and mortgage debtors: after a creditor files MFRS, if the debtor voluntarily dismisses to avoid an adverse ruling, the 180-day bar kicks in automatically - no court order needed.

See 109(g) dismissal bar.

Dismissal With Prejudice in Arkansas

Separate from the statutory 180 days, Arkansas bankruptcy courts can dismiss a case "with prejudice" under 11 U.S.C. Section 349(a) and bar refiling for a longer period - commonly 1 year, 2 years, or (rarely) permanently.

Typical triggers in Arkansas practice:

Serial filings designed to stop foreclosure without any plan of reorganization.

Failure to make plan payments repeatedly across multiple cases.

Bad-faith filings where the petition was not accompanied by schedules or where schedules contained materially false statements.

Dismissal with prejudice orders bind the debtor under res judicata and must be vacated (via Rule 60(b)) before any refile.

Arkansas Federal Bankruptcy Data

Refile timing in Arkansas depends on both the federal statute and the local dismissal/relief-from-stay practices reflected in the case data.

Was the prior case discharged? If Chapter 7 discharged, 727(a)(8) controls (8 years Ch7 to Ch7; 1328(f) applies to Ch13 after Ch7 at 4 years). If Chapter 13 discharged, 1328(f)(2) bars another Ch13 discharge for 2 years.

Was there a sanctions order in the prior case? Some Arkansas judges enter injunctions against refiling under 105(a) as part of sanctions, independent of 109(g) and 349.

"Chapter 20" is the informal name for filing Chapter 7 to discharge unsecured debt, then filing Chapter 13 immediately after to restructure a mortgage, vehicle loan, or priority tax debt even though 1328(f) bars a second discharge.

In a Arkansas Chapter 20, the second-case Chapter 13 plan:

Strips wholly-unsecured junior mortgages where state valuation supports it.

Pays priority taxes and secured vehicle loans through the plan.

Does not result in a discharge at completion - but reorganization still proceeds.

For Arkansas's high-dismissal chapter 13 environment, the Chapter 20 path often works better than a single Chapter 13 when substantial unsecured debt exists.

Corporate and Small-Business Refile Constraints

Note: entity debtors (LLCs, corporations) generally cannot file pro se - they must be represented by counsel to handle plan-level matters. This is a practical constraint on any refile strategy where the debtor is a business entity rather than an individual.

See corporate refile rules for the Sub V reorganization refile and the rules on pre-confirmation versus post-confirmation filings.

Pays priority taxes and secured vehicle loans through the plan.

Does not result in a discharge at completion - but reorganization still proceeds.

For Connecticut's high-dismissal chapter 13 environment, the Chapter 20 path often works better than a single Chapter 13 when substantial unsecured debt exists.

Corporate and Small-Business Refile Constraints

Note: entity debtors (LLCs, corporations) generally cannot file pro se - they must be represented by counsel to handle plan-level matters. This is a practical constraint on any refile strategy where the debtor is a business entity rather than an individual.

See corporate refile rules for the Sub V reorganization refile and the rules on pre-confirmation versus post-confirmation filings.

## Can I File Bankruptcy Again in Delaware? [2026] Refile Timing Rules
Source: https://canifileagain.org/states/delaware.html

← canifileagain.org home

Can I File Bankruptcy Again in Delaware? [2026] Refile Timing Rules

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Delaware residents.

Can You File Bankruptcy Again in Delaware?

Yes - but the timing depends on three separate federal statutes and the reason your prior case ended. This page walks through each bar for Delaware filers.

Section 727(a)(8) - 8-year bar on a second Chapter 7 discharge after a prior Chapter 7 discharge.

Section 1328(f) - 4-year bar on a Chapter 13 discharge when the prior case was a Chapter 7/11/12 discharge (measured from the filing date of the prior case, not the discharge date).

Section 109(g) - 180-day bar on any new filing when the prior case was dismissed for willful failure to abide by court orders or was voluntarily dismissed after a motion for relief from stay.

Delaware's bankruptcy court is well-known for business cases, but consumer 109(g) rulings follow 3rd Circuit precedent.

Section 727(a)(8): The 8-Year Chapter 7-After-Chapter 7 Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 727(a)(8), a Chapter 7 debtor cannot receive a second Chapter 7 discharge within 8 years of filing the prior case that produced a discharge.

The 8 years runs from filing date to filing date, not discharge to filing.

If the prior case was dismissed rather than discharged, 727(a)(8) does not bar the refile - but 109(g) might.

A Delaware filer whose prior Chapter 7 was filed January 1, 2018, can file a new Chapter 7 on or after January 1, 2026.

See the 727(a)(8) eight-year rule for the full mechanics.

Section 1328(f): The 4-Year Chapter 13-After-Chapter 7 Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 1328(f)(1), a Chapter 13 debtor cannot receive a discharge if a Chapter 7, 11, or 12 discharge was entered in a case filed within 4 years before the current filing.

This is the so-called "Chapter 20" strategy: filing Chapter 7 first for unsecured-debt discharge, then Chapter 13 to cram down or cure secured debt. The Chapter 13 can still be filed before the 4 years, but without a discharge at completion.

Section 1328(f)(2) adds a 2-year bar on Chapter 13 after a prior Chapter 13 discharge.

4 years is from filing date of prior case to filing date of new case, not discharge date.

For Delaware filers considering the Chapter 20 route, the 4-year bar is a planning constraint, not an absolute stopper - many debtors file the second case intentionally knowing a no-discharge plan still works.

See the 1328(f) four-year rule for a worked example.

Section 109(g): The 180-Day Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 109(g), a debtor cannot be a debtor in any chapter for 180 days after a prior case is dismissed if either:

109(g)(1) - the case was dismissed for "willful failure" to abide by court orders or to appear in proper prosecution of the case; or

109(g)(2) - the debtor voluntarily dismissed the case after a creditor filed a motion for relief from the automatic stay (MFRS).

DE chapter 7 discharge rates are high.

109(g)(2) is the most common trap for Delaware vehicle-loan and mortgage debtors: after a creditor files MFRS, if the debtor voluntarily dismisses to avoid an adverse ruling, the 180-day bar kicks in automatically - no court order needed.

See 109(g) dismissal bar.

Dismissal With Prejudice in Delaware

Separate from the statutory 180 days, Delaware bankruptcy courts can dismiss a case "with prejudice" under 11 U.S.C. Section 349(a) and bar refiling for a longer period - commonly 1 year, 2 years, or (rarely) permanently.

Typical triggers in Delaware practice:

Serial filings designed to stop foreclosure without any plan of reorganization.

Failure to make plan payments repeatedly across multiple cases.

Bad-faith filings where the petition was not accompanied by schedules or where schedules contained materially false statements.

Dismissal with prejudice orders bind the debtor under res judicata and must be vacated (via Rule 60(b)) before any refile.

Stacking the Three Bars in Delaware

For a Delaware filer considering a second case, all three bars must be checked together:

Was the prior case discharged? If Chapter 7 discharged, 727(a)(8) controls (8 years Ch7 to Ch7; 1328(f) applies to Ch13 after Ch7 at 4 years). If Chapter 13 discharged, 1328(f)(2) bars another Ch13 discharge for 2 years.

Was the prior case dismissed? Check 109(g)(1) willful-failure ground and 109(g)(2) MFRS-voluntary-dismissal ground. Check the dismissal order for any "with prejudice" language.

Was there a sanctions order in the prior case? Some Delaware judges enter injunctions against refiling under 105(a) as part of sanctions, independent of 109(g) and 349.

Run our refile-timing calculator to see your earliest allowable refile date.

Delaware Chapter 20 Strategy

"Chapter 20" is the informal name for filing Chapter 7 to discharge unsecured debt, then filing Chapter 13 immediately after to restructure a mortgage, vehicle loan, or priority tax debt even though 1328(f) bars a second discharge.

In a Delaware Chapter 20, the second-case Chapter 13 plan:

Cures mortgage arrears under 1322(b)(5) over the plan term.

Strips wholly-unsecured junior mortgages where state valuation supports it.

Pays priority taxes and secured vehicle loans through the plan.

Does not result in a discharge at completion - but reorganization still proceeds.

For Delaware's high-dismissal chapter 13 environment, the Chapter 20 path often works better than a single Chapter 13 when substantial unsecured debt exists.

Corporate and Small-Business Refile Constraints

Note: entity debtors (LLCs, corporations) generally cannot file pro se - they must be represented by counsel to handle plan-level matters. This is a practical constraint on any refile strategy where the debtor is a business entity rather than an individual.

See corporate refile rules for the Sub V reorganization refile and the rules on pre-confirmation versus post-confirmation filings.

Related Delaware Resources

1328(f) four-year bar

109(g) 180-day bar

If the prior case was dismissed rather than discharged, 727(a)(8) does not bar the refile - but 109(g) might.

A Hawaii filer whose prior Chapter 7 was filed January 1, 2018, can file a new Chapter 7 on or after January 1, 2026.

See the 727(a)(8) eight-year rule for the full mechanics.

Section 1328(f): The 4-Year Chapter 13-After-Chapter 7 Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 1328(f)(1), a Chapter 13 debtor cannot receive a discharge if a Chapter 7, 11, or 12 discharge was entered in a case filed within 4 years before the current filing.

This is the so-called "Chapter 20" strategy: filing Chapter 7 first for unsecured-debt discharge, then Chapter 13 to cram down or cure secured debt. The Chapter 13 can still be filed before the 4 years, but without a discharge at completion.

Section 1328(f)(2) adds a 2-year bar on Chapter 13 after a prior Chapter 13 discharge.

4 years is from filing date of prior case to filing date of new case, not discharge date.

For Hawaii filers considering the Chapter 20 route, the 4-year bar is a planning constraint, not an absolute stopper - many debtors file the second case intentionally knowing a no-discharge plan still works.

See the 1328(f) four-year rule for a worked example.

Section 109(g): The 180-Day Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 109(g), a debtor cannot be a debtor in any chapter for 180 days after a prior case is dismissed if either:

109(g)(1) - the case was dismissed for "willful failure" to abide by court orders or to appear in proper prosecution of the case; or

109(g)(2) - the debtor voluntarily dismissed the case after a creditor filed a motion for relief from the automatic stay (MFRS).

9th Circuit authority applies.

109(g)(2) is the most common trap for Hawaii vehicle-loan and mortgage debtors: after a creditor files MFRS, if the debtor voluntarily dismisses to avoid an adverse ruling, the 180-day bar kicks in automatically - no court order needed.

See 109(g) dismissal bar.

Dismissal With Prejudice in Hawaii

Separate from the statutory 180 days, Hawaii bankruptcy courts can dismiss a case "with prejudice" under 11 U.S.C. Section 349(a) and bar refiling for a longer period - commonly 1 year, 2 years, or (rarely) permanently.

Typical triggers in Hawaii practice:

Serial filings designed to stop foreclosure without any plan of reorganization.

Failure to make plan payments repeatedly across multiple cases.

Bad-faith filings where the petition was not accompanied by schedules or where schedules contained materially false statements.

Dismissal with prejudice orders bind the debtor under res judicata and must be vacated (via Rule 60(b)) before any refile.

Stacking the Three Bars in Hawaii

For a Hawaii filer considering a second case, all three bars must be checked together:

Was the prior case discharged? If Chapter 7 discharged, 727(a)(8) controls (8 years Ch7 to Ch7; 1328(f) applies to Ch13 after Ch7 at 4 years). If Chapter 13 discharged, 1328(f)(2) bars another Ch13 discharge for 2 years.

Was the prior case dismissed? Check 109(g)(1) willful-failure ground and 109(g)(2) MFRS-voluntary-dismissal ground. Check the dismissal order for any "with prejudice" language.

Was there a sanctions order in the prior case? Some Hawaii judges enter injunctions against refiling under 105(a) as part of sanctions, independent of 109(g) and 349.

Run our refile-timing calculator to see your earliest allowable refile date.

Hawaii Chapter 20 Strategy

"Chapter 20" is the informal name for filing Chapter 7 to discharge unsecured debt, then filing Chapter 13 immediately after to restructure a mortgage, vehicle loan, or priority tax debt even though 1328(f) bars a second discharge.

In a Hawaii Chapter 20, the second-case Chapter 13 plan:

Cures mortgage arrears under 1322(b)(5) over the plan term.

Strips wholly-unsecured junior mortgages where state valuation supports it.

Pays priority taxes and secured vehicle loans through the plan.

Does not result in a discharge at completion - but reorganization still proceeds.

For Hawaii's high-dismissal chapter 13 environment, the Chapter 20 path often works better than a single Chapter 13 when substantial unsecured debt exists.

Corporate and Small-Business Refile Constraints

Note: entity debtors (LLCs, corporations) generally cannot file pro se - they must be represented by counsel to handle plan-level matters. This is a practical constraint on any refile strategy where the debtor is a business entity rather than an individual.

See corporate refile rules for the Sub V reorganization refile and the rules on pre-confirmation versus post-confirmation filings.

See 109(g) dismissal bar.

Dismissal With Prejudice in Iowa

Separate from the statutory 180 days, Iowa bankruptcy courts can dismiss a case "with prejudice" under 11 U.S.C. Section 349(a) and bar refiling for a longer period - commonly 1 year, 2 years, or (rarely) permanently.

Typical triggers in Iowa practice:

Serial filings designed to stop foreclosure without any plan of reorganization.

Failure to make plan payments repeatedly across multiple cases.

Bad-faith filings where the petition was not accompanied by schedules or where schedules contained materially false statements.

Dismissal with prejudice orders bind the debtor under res judicata and must be vacated (via Rule 60(b)) before any refile.

Stacking the Three Bars in Iowa

For a Iowa filer considering a second case, all three bars must be checked together:

Was the prior case discharged? If Chapter 7 discharged, 727(a)(8) controls (8 years Ch7 to Ch7; 1328(f) applies to Ch13 after Ch7 at 4 years). If Chapter 13 discharged, 1328(f)(2) bars another Ch13 discharge for 2 years.

Was the prior case dismissed? Check 109(g)(1) willful-failure ground and 109(g)(2) MFRS-voluntary-dismissal ground. Check the dismissal order for any "with prejudice" language.

Was there a sanctions order in the prior case? Some Iowa judges enter injunctions against refiling under 105(a) as part of sanctions, independent of 109(g) and 349.

Run our refile-timing calculator to see your earliest allowable refile date.

Iowa Chapter 20 Strategy

"Chapter 20" is the informal name for filing Chapter 7 to discharge unsecured debt, then filing Chapter 13 immediately after to restructure a mortgage, vehicle loan, or priority tax debt even though 1328(f) bars a second discharge.

In a Iowa Chapter 20, the second-case Chapter 13 plan:

Cures mortgage arrears under 1322(b)(5) over the plan term.

Strips wholly-unsecured junior mortgages where state valuation supports it.

Pays priority taxes and secured vehicle loans through the plan.

Does not result in a discharge at completion - but reorganization still proceeds.

For Iowa's high-dismissal chapter 13 environment, the Chapter 20 path often works better than a single Chapter 13 when substantial unsecured debt exists.

Corporate and Small-Business Refile Constraints

Note: entity debtors (LLCs, corporations) generally cannot file pro se - they must be represented by counsel to handle plan-level matters. This is a practical constraint on any refile strategy where the debtor is a business entity rather than an individual.

See corporate refile rules for the Sub V reorganization refile and the rules on pre-confirmation versus post-confirmation filings.

## Can I File Bankruptcy Again in Kansas? [2026] Refile Timing Rules
Source: https://canifileagain.org/states/kansas.html

← canifileagain.org home

Can I File Bankruptcy Again in Kansas? [2026] Refile Timing Rules

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Kansas residents.

Can You File Bankruptcy Again in Kansas?

Yes - but the timing depends on three separate federal statutes and the reason your prior case ended. This page walks through each bar for Kansas filers.

Section 727(a)(8) - 8-year bar on a second Chapter 7 discharge after a prior Chapter 7 discharge.

Section 1328(f) - 4-year bar on a Chapter 13 discharge when the prior case was a Chapter 7/11/12 discharge (measured from the filing date of the prior case, not the discharge date).

Section 109(g) - 180-day bar on any new filing when the prior case was dismissed for willful failure to abide by court orders or was voluntarily dismissed after a motion for relief from stay.

Kansas bankruptcy court applies 10th Circuit 109(g) standards. Dismissal-with-prejudice orders may bar refiling for 1-2 years.

Section 727(a)(8): The 8-Year Chapter 7-After-Chapter 7 Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 727(a)(8), a Chapter 7 debtor cannot receive a second Chapter 7 discharge within 8 years of filing the prior case that produced a discharge.

The 8 years runs from filing date to filing date, not discharge to filing.

If the prior case was dismissed rather than discharged, 727(a)(8) does not bar the refile - but 109(g) might.

A Kansas filer whose prior Chapter 7 was filed January 1, 2018, can file a new Chapter 7 on or after January 1, 2026.

See the 727(a)(8) eight-year rule for the full mechanics.

Section 1328(f): The 4-Year Chapter 13-After-Chapter 7 Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 1328(f)(1), a Chapter 13 debtor cannot receive a discharge if a Chapter 7, 11, or 12 discharge was entered in a case filed within 4 years before the current filing.

This is the so-called "Chapter 20" strategy: filing Chapter 7 first for unsecured-debt discharge, then Chapter 13 to cram down or cure secured debt. The Chapter 13 can still be filed before the 4 years, but without a discharge at completion.

Section 1328(f)(2) adds a 2-year bar on Chapter 13 after a prior Chapter 13 discharge.

4 years is from filing date of prior case to filing date of new case, not discharge date.

For Kansas filers considering the Chapter 20 route, the 4-year bar is a planning constraint, not an absolute stopper - many debtors file the second case intentionally knowing a no-discharge plan still works.

See the 1328(f) four-year rule for a worked example.

Section 109(g): The 180-Day Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 109(g), a debtor cannot be a debtor in any chapter for 180 days after a prior case is dismissed if either:

109(g)(1) - the case was dismissed for "willful failure" to abide by court orders or to appear in proper prosecution of the case; or

109(g)(2) - the debtor voluntarily dismissed the case after a creditor filed a motion for relief from the automatic stay (MFRS).

KS has one federal bankruptcy district; chapter 13 dismissal rates are mid-range.

109(g)(2) is the most common trap for Kansas vehicle-loan and mortgage debtors: after a creditor files MFRS, if the debtor voluntarily dismisses to avoid an adverse ruling, the 180-day bar kicks in automatically - no court order needed.

See 109(g) dismissal bar.

Dismissal With Prejudice in Kansas

Separate from the statutory 180 days, Kansas bankruptcy courts can dismiss a case "with prejudice" under 11 U.S.C. Section 349(a) and bar refiling for a longer period - commonly 1 year, 2 years, or (rarely) permanently.

Typical triggers in Kansas practice:

Serial filings designed to stop foreclosure without any plan of reorganization.

Failure to make plan payments repeatedly across multiple cases.

Bad-faith filings where the petition was not accompanied by schedules or where schedules contained materially false statements.

Dismissal with prejudice orders bind the debtor under res judicata and must be vacated (via Rule 60(b)) before any refile.

Kansas Federal Bankruptcy Data

Refile timing in Kansas depends on both the federal statute and the local dismissal/relief-from-stay practices reflected in the case data.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 40,849 consumer bankruptcy cases from Kansas's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 718,67399.4%0.5%

Chapter 1322,17673.1%26.9%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Stacking the Three Bars in Kansas

For a Kansas filer considering a second case, all three bars must be checked together:

Was the prior case discharged? If Chapter 7 discharged, 727(a)(8) controls (8 years Ch7 to Ch7; 1328(f) applies to Ch13 after Ch7 at 4 years). If Chapter 13 discharged, 1328(f)(2) bars another Ch13 discharge for 2 years.

Was the prior case dismissed? Check 109(g)(1) willful-failure ground and 109(g)(2) MFRS-voluntary-dismissal ground. Check the dismissal order for any "with prejudice" language.

Was there a sanctions order in the prior case? Some Kansas judges enter injunctions against refiling under 105(a) as part of sanctions, independent of 109(g) and 349.

Run our refile-timing calculator to see your earliest allowable refile date.

Kansas Chapter 20 Strategy

"Chapter 20" is the informal name for filing Chapter 7 to discharge unsecured debt, then filing Chapter 13 immediately after to restructure a mortgage, vehicle loan, or priority tax debt even though 1328(f) bars a second discharge.

In a Kansas Chapter 20, the second-case Chapter 13 plan:

Cures mortgage arrears under 1322(b)(5) over the plan term.

Strips wholly-unsecured junior mortgages where state valuation supports it.

Pays priority taxes and secured vehicle loans through the plan.

Does not result in a discharge at completion - but reorganization still proceeds.

For Kansas's high-dismissal chapter 13 environment, the Chapter 20 path often works better than a single Chapter 13 when substantial unsecured debt exists.

Corporate and Small-Business Refile Constraints

Note: entity debtors (LLCs, corporations) generally cannot file pro se - they must be represented by counsel to handle plan-level matters. This is a practical constraint on any refile strategy where the debtor is a business entity rather than an individual.

See corporate refile rules for the Sub V reorganization refile and the rules on pre-confirmation versus post-confirmation filings.

## Can I File Bankruptcy Again in Maryland? [2026] Refile Timing Rules
Source: https://canifileagain.org/states/maryland.html

← canifileagain.org home

Can I File Bankruptcy Again in Maryland? [2026] Refile Timing Rules

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Maryland residents.

Can You File Bankruptcy Again in Maryland?

Yes - but the timing depends on three separate federal statutes and the reason your prior case ended. This page walks through each bar for Maryland filers.

Section 727(a)(8) - 8-year bar on a second Chapter 7 discharge after a prior Chapter 7 discharge.

Section 1328(f) - 4-year bar on a Chapter 13 discharge when the prior case was a Chapter 7/11/12 discharge (measured from the filing date of the prior case, not the discharge date).

Section 109(g) - 180-day bar on any new filing when the prior case was dismissed for willful failure to abide by court orders or was voluntarily dismissed after a motion for relief from stay.

Maryland bankruptcy court applies 4th Circuit 109(g) standards. Baltimore and Greenbelt divisions handle high volume.

Section 727(a)(8): The 8-Year Chapter 7-After-Chapter 7 Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 727(a)(8), a Chapter 7 debtor cannot receive a second Chapter 7 discharge within 8 years of filing the prior case that produced a discharge.

The 8 years runs from filing date to filing date, not discharge to filing.

If the prior case was dismissed rather than discharged, 727(a)(8) does not bar the refile - but 109(g) might.

A Maryland filer whose prior Chapter 7 was filed January 1, 2018, can file a new Chapter 7 on or after January 1, 2026.

See the 727(a)(8) eight-year rule for the full mechanics.

Section 1328(f): The 4-Year Chapter 13-After-Chapter 7 Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 1328(f)(1), a Chapter 13 debtor cannot receive a discharge if a Chapter 7, 11, or 12 discharge was entered in a case filed within 4 years before the current filing.

This is the so-called "Chapter 20" strategy: filing Chapter 7 first for unsecured-debt discharge, then Chapter 13 to cram down or cure secured debt. The Chapter 13 can still be filed before the 4 years, but without a discharge at completion.

Section 1328(f)(2) adds a 2-year bar on Chapter 13 after a prior Chapter 13 discharge.

4 years is from filing date of prior case to filing date of new case, not discharge date.

For Maryland filers considering the Chapter 20 route, the 4-year bar is a planning constraint, not an absolute stopper - many debtors file the second case intentionally knowing a no-discharge plan still works.

See the 1328(f) four-year rule for a worked example.

Section 109(g): The 180-Day Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 109(g), a debtor cannot be a debtor in any chapter for 180 days after a prior case is dismissed if either:

109(g)(1) - the case was dismissed for "willful failure" to abide by court orders or to appear in proper prosecution of the case; or

109(g)(2) - the debtor voluntarily dismissed the case after a creditor filed a motion for relief from the automatic stay (MFRS).

MD chapter 13 dismissal rates moderate.

109(g)(2) is the most common trap for Maryland vehicle-loan and mortgage debtors: after a creditor files MFRS, if the debtor voluntarily dismisses to avoid an adverse ruling, the 180-day bar kicks in automatically - no court order needed.

See 109(g) dismissal bar.

Dismissal With Prejudice in Maryland

Separate from the statutory 180 days, Maryland bankruptcy courts can dismiss a case "with prejudice" under 11 U.S.C. Section 349(a) and bar refiling for a longer period - commonly 1 year, 2 years, or (rarely) permanently.

Typical triggers in Maryland practice:

Serial filings designed to stop foreclosure without any plan of reorganization.

Failure to make plan payments repeatedly across multiple cases.

Bad-faith filings where the petition was not accompanied by schedules or where schedules contained materially false statements.

Dismissal with prejudice orders bind the debtor under res judicata and must be vacated (via Rule 60(b)) before any refile.

Maryland Federal Bankruptcy Data

Refile timing in Maryland depends on both the federal statute and the local dismissal/relief-from-stay practices reflected in the case data.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 559 consumer bankruptcy cases from Maryland's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 742097.4%0.0%

Chapter 13139n/an/a

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Stacking the Three Bars in Maryland

For a Maryland filer considering a second case, all three bars must be checked together:

Was the prior case discharged? If Chapter 7 discharged, 727(a)(8) controls (8 years Ch7 to Ch7; 1328(f) applies to Ch13 after Ch7 at 4 years). If Chapter 13 discharged, 1328(f)(2) bars another Ch13 discharge for 2 years.

Was the prior case dismissed? Check 109(g)(1) willful-failure ground and 109(g)(2) MFRS-voluntary-dismissal ground. Check the dismissal order for any "with prejudice" language.

Was there a sanctions order in the prior case? Some Maryland judges enter injunctions against refiling under 105(a) as part of sanctions, independent of 109(g) and 349.

Run our refile-timing calculator to see your earliest allowable refile date.

Maryland Chapter 20 Strategy

"Chapter 20" is the informal name for filing Chapter 7 to discharge unsecured debt, then filing Chapter 13 immediately after to restructure a mortgage, vehicle loan, or priority tax debt even though 1328(f) bars a second discharge.

In a Maryland Chapter 20, the second-case Chapter 13 plan:

Cures mortgage arrears under 1322(b)(5) over the plan term.

Strips wholly-unsecured junior mortgages where state valuation supports it.

Pays priority taxes and secured vehicle loans through the plan.

Does not result in a discharge at completion - but reorganization still proceeds.

For Maryland's high-dismissal chapter 13 environment, the Chapter 20 path often works better than a single Chapter 13 when substantial unsecured debt exists.

Corporate and Small-Business Refile Constraints

Note: entity debtors (LLCs, corporations) generally cannot file pro se - they must be represented by counsel to handle plan-level matters. This is a practical constraint on any refile strategy where the debtor is a business entity rather than an individual.

See corporate refile rules for the Sub V reorganization refile and the rules on pre-confirmation versus post-confirmation filings.

1328(f) four-year bar

109(g) 180-day bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 109(g), a debtor cannot be a debtor in any chapter for 180 days after a prior case is dismissed if either:

109(g)(1) - the case was dismissed for "willful failure" to abide by court orders or to appear in proper prosecution of the case; or

109(g)(2) - the debtor voluntarily dismissed the case after a creditor filed a motion for relief from the automatic stay (MFRS).

MS chapter 13 dismissal rates are very high.

109(g)(2) is the most common trap for Mississippi vehicle-loan and mortgage debtors: after a creditor files MFRS, if the debtor voluntarily dismisses to avoid an adverse ruling, the 180-day bar kicks in automatically - no court order needed.

See 109(g) dismissal bar.

Dismissal With Prejudice in Mississippi

Separate from the statutory 180 days, Mississippi bankruptcy courts can dismiss a case "with prejudice" under 11 U.S.C. Section 349(a) and bar refiling for a longer period - commonly 1 year, 2 years, or (rarely) permanently.

Typical triggers in Mississippi practice:

Serial filings designed to stop foreclosure without any plan of reorganization.

Failure to make plan payments repeatedly across multiple cases.

Bad-faith filings where the petition was not accompanied by schedules or where schedules contained materially false statements.

Dismissal with prejudice orders bind the debtor under res judicata and must be vacated (via Rule 60(b)) before any refile.

Stacking the Three Bars in Mississippi

For a Mississippi filer considering a second case, all three bars must be checked together:

Was the prior case discharged? If Chapter 7 discharged, 727(a)(8) controls (8 years Ch7 to Ch7; 1328(f) applies to Ch13 after Ch7 at 4 years). If Chapter 13 discharged, 1328(f)(2) bars another Ch13 discharge for 2 years.

Was the prior case dismissed? Check 109(g)(1) willful-failure ground and 109(g)(2) MFRS-voluntary-dismissal ground. Check the dismissal order for any "with prejudice" language.

Was there a sanctions order in the prior case? Some Mississippi judges enter injunctions against refiling under 105(a) as part of sanctions, independent of 109(g) and 349.

Run our refile-timing calculator to see your earliest allowable refile date.

Mississippi Chapter 20 Strategy

"Chapter 20" is the informal name for filing Chapter 7 to discharge unsecured debt, then filing Chapter 13 immediately after to restructure a mortgage, vehicle loan, or priority tax debt even though 1328(f) bars a second discharge.

In a Mississippi Chapter 20, the second-case Chapter 13 plan:

Cures mortgage arrears under 1322(b)(5) over the plan term.

Strips wholly-unsecured junior mortgages where state valuation supports it.

Pays priority taxes and secured vehicle loans through the plan.

Does not result in a discharge at completion - but reorganization still proceeds.

For Mississippi's high-dismissal chapter 13 environment, the Chapter 20 path often works better than a single Chapter 13 when substantial unsecured debt exists.

Corporate and Small-Business Refile Constraints

Note: entity debtors (LLCs, corporations) generally cannot file pro se - they must be represented by counsel to handle plan-level matters. This is a practical constraint on any refile strategy where the debtor is a business entity rather than an individual.

See corporate refile rules for the Sub V reorganization refile and the rules on pre-confirmation versus post-confirmation filings.

## Can I File Bankruptcy Again in Missouri? [2026] Refile Timing Rules
Source: https://canifileagain.org/states/missouri.html

← canifileagain.org home

Can I File Bankruptcy Again in Missouri? [2026] Refile Timing Rules

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Missouri residents.

Can You File Bankruptcy Again in Missouri?

Yes - but the timing depends on three separate federal statutes and the reason your prior case ended. This page walks through each bar for Missouri filers.

Section 727(a)(8) - 8-year bar on a second Chapter 7 discharge after a prior Chapter 7 discharge.

Section 1328(f) - 4-year bar on a Chapter 13 discharge when the prior case was a Chapter 7/11/12 discharge (measured from the filing date of the prior case, not the discharge date).

Section 109(g) - 180-day bar on any new filing when the prior case was dismissed for willful failure to abide by court orders or was voluntarily dismissed after a motion for relief from stay.

Missouri bankruptcy courts (Eastern, Western) apply 8th Circuit 109(g) standards. Kansas City (W.D. Mo.) and St. Louis (E.D. Mo.) both see active 109(g) motions.

Section 727(a)(8): The 8-Year Chapter 7-After-Chapter 7 Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 727(a)(8), a Chapter 7 debtor cannot receive a second Chapter 7 discharge within 8 years of filing the prior case that produced a discharge.

The 8 years runs from filing date to filing date, not discharge to filing.

If the prior case was dismissed rather than discharged, 727(a)(8) does not bar the refile - but 109(g) might.

A Missouri filer whose prior Chapter 7 was filed January 1, 2018, can file a new Chapter 7 on or after January 1, 2026.

See the 727(a)(8) eight-year rule for the full mechanics.

Section 1328(f): The 4-Year Chapter 13-After-Chapter 7 Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 1328(f)(1), a Chapter 13 debtor cannot receive a discharge if a Chapter 7, 11, or 12 discharge was entered in a case filed within 4 years before the current filing.

This is the so-called "Chapter 20" strategy: filing Chapter 7 first for unsecured-debt discharge, then Chapter 13 to cram down or cure secured debt. The Chapter 13 can still be filed before the 4 years, but without a discharge at completion.

Section 1328(f)(2) adds a 2-year bar on Chapter 13 after a prior Chapter 13 discharge.

4 years is from filing date of prior case to filing date of new case, not discharge date.

For Missouri filers considering the Chapter 20 route, the 4-year bar is a planning constraint, not an absolute stopper - many debtors file the second case intentionally knowing a no-discharge plan still works.

See the 1328(f) four-year rule for a worked example.

Section 109(g): The 180-Day Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 109(g), a debtor cannot be a debtor in any chapter for 180 days after a prior case is dismissed if either:

109(g)(1) - the case was dismissed for "willful failure" to abide by court orders or to appear in proper prosecution of the case; or

109(g)(2) - the debtor voluntarily dismissed the case after a creditor filed a motion for relief from the automatic stay (MFRS).

MO chapter 13 dismissal rates are relatively high.

109(g)(2) is the most common trap for Missouri vehicle-loan and mortgage debtors: after a creditor files MFRS, if the debtor voluntarily dismisses to avoid an adverse ruling, the 180-day bar kicks in automatically - no court order needed.

See 109(g) dismissal bar.

Dismissal With Prejudice in Missouri

Separate from the statutory 180 days, Missouri bankruptcy courts can dismiss a case "with prejudice" under 11 U.S.C. Section 349(a) and bar refiling for a longer period - commonly 1 year, 2 years, or (rarely) permanently.

Typical triggers in Missouri practice:

Serial filings designed to stop foreclosure without any plan of reorganization.

Failure to make plan payments repeatedly across multiple cases.

Bad-faith filings where the petition was not accompanied by schedules or where schedules contained materially false statements.

Dismissal with prejudice orders bind the debtor under res judicata and must be vacated (via Rule 60(b)) before any refile.

Missouri Federal Bankruptcy Data

Refile timing in Missouri depends on both the federal statute and the local dismissal/relief-from-stay practices reflected in the case data.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 45,771 consumer bankruptcy cases from Missouri's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 722,13299.0%0.8%

Chapter 1323,63955.1%44.7%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Stacking the Three Bars in Missouri

For a Missouri filer considering a second case, all three bars must be checked together:

Was the prior case discharged? If Chapter 7 discharged, 727(a)(8) controls (8 years Ch7 to Ch7; 1328(f) applies to Ch13 after Ch7 at 4 years). If Chapter 13 discharged, 1328(f)(2) bars another Ch13 discharge for 2 years.

Was the prior case dismissed? Check 109(g)(1) willful-failure ground and 109(g)(2) MFRS-voluntary-dismissal ground. Check the dismissal order for any "with prejudice" language.

Was there a sanctions order in the prior case? Some Missouri judges enter injunctions against refiling under 105(a) as part of sanctions, independent of 109(g) and 349.

Run our refile-timing calculator to see your earliest allowable refile date.

Missouri Chapter 20 Strategy

"Chapter 20" is the informal name for filing Chapter 7 to discharge unsecured debt, then filing Chapter 13 immediately after to restructure a mortgage, vehicle loan, or priority tax debt even though 1328(f) bars a second discharge.

In a Missouri Chapter 20, the second-case Chapter 13 plan:

Cures mortgage arrears under 1322(b)(5) over the plan term.

Strips wholly-unsecured junior mortgages where state valuation supports it.

Pays priority taxes and secured vehicle loans through the plan.

Does not result in a discharge at completion - but reorganization still proceeds.

For Missouri's high-dismissal chapter 13 environment, the Chapter 20 path often works better than a single Chapter 13 when substantial unsecured debt exists.

Corporate and Small-Business Refile Constraints

Note: entity debtors (LLCs, corporations) generally cannot file pro se - they must be represented by counsel to handle plan-level matters. This is a practical constraint on any refile strategy where the debtor is a business entity rather than an individual.

See corporate refile rules for the Sub V reorganization refile and the rules on pre-confirmation versus post-confirmation filings.

See corporate refile rules for the Sub V reorganization refile and the rules on pre-confirmation versus post-confirmation filings.
