## Can I File Bankruptcy Again in New Hampshire? [2026] Refile Timing Rules
Source: https://canifileagain.org/states/new-hampshire.html

← canifileagain.org home

Can I File Bankruptcy Again in New Hampshire? [2026] Refile Timing Rules

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for New Hampshire residents.

Can You File Bankruptcy Again in New Hampshire?

Yes - but the timing depends on three separate federal statutes and the reason your prior case ended. This page walks through each bar for New Hampshire filers.

Section 727(a)(8) - 8-year bar on a second Chapter 7 discharge after a prior Chapter 7 discharge.

Section 1328(f) - 4-year bar on a Chapter 13 discharge when the prior case was a Chapter 7/11/12 discharge (measured from the filing date of the prior case, not the discharge date).

Section 109(g) - 180-day bar on any new filing when the prior case was dismissed for willful failure to abide by court orders or was voluntarily dismissed after a motion for relief from stay.

New Hampshire bankruptcy court applies 1st Circuit 109(g) standards. Low volume; 109(g) rulings fact-specific.

Section 727(a)(8): The 8-Year Chapter 7-After-Chapter 7 Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 727(a)(8), a Chapter 7 debtor cannot receive a second Chapter 7 discharge within 8 years of filing the prior case that produced a discharge.

The 8 years runs from filing date to filing date, not discharge to filing.

If the prior case was dismissed rather than discharged, 727(a)(8) does not bar the refile - but 109(g) might.

A New Hampshire filer whose prior Chapter 7 was filed January 1, 2018, can file a new Chapter 7 on or after January 1, 2026.

See the 727(a)(8) eight-year rule for the full mechanics.

Section 1328(f): The 4-Year Chapter 13-After-Chapter 7 Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 1328(f)(1), a Chapter 13 debtor cannot receive a discharge if a Chapter 7, 11, or 12 discharge was entered in a case filed within 4 years before the current filing.

This is the so-called "Chapter 20" strategy: filing Chapter 7 first for unsecured-debt discharge, then Chapter 13 to cram down or cure secured debt. The Chapter 13 can still be filed before the 4 years, but without a discharge at completion.

Section 1328(f)(2) adds a 2-year bar on Chapter 13 after a prior Chapter 13 discharge.

4 years is from filing date of prior case to filing date of new case, not discharge date.

For New Hampshire filers considering the Chapter 20 route, the 4-year bar is a planning constraint, not an absolute stopper - many debtors file the second case intentionally knowing a no-discharge plan still works.

See the 1328(f) four-year rule for a worked example.

Section 109(g): The 180-Day Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 109(g), a debtor cannot be a debtor in any chapter for 180 days after a prior case is dismissed if either:

109(g)(1) - the case was dismissed for "willful failure" to abide by court orders or to appear in proper prosecution of the case; or

109(g)(2) - the debtor voluntarily dismissed the case after a creditor filed a motion for relief from the automatic stay (MFRS).

NH has one federal bankruptcy district.

109(g)(2) is the most common trap for New Hampshire vehicle-loan and mortgage debtors: after a creditor files MFRS, if the debtor voluntarily dismisses to avoid an adverse ruling, the 180-day bar kicks in automatically - no court order needed.

See 109(g) dismissal bar.

Dismissal With Prejudice in New Hampshire

Separate from the statutory 180 days, New Hampshire bankruptcy courts can dismiss a case "with prejudice" under 11 U.S.C. Section 349(a) and bar refiling for a longer period - commonly 1 year, 2 years, or (rarely) permanently.

Typical triggers in New Hampshire practice:

Serial filings designed to stop foreclosure without any plan of reorganization.

Failure to make plan payments repeatedly across multiple cases.

Bad-faith filings where the petition was not accompanied by schedules or where schedules contained materially false statements.

Dismissal with prejudice orders bind the debtor under res judicata and must be vacated (via Rule 60(b)) before any refile.

Stacking the Three Bars in New Hampshire

For a New Hampshire filer considering a second case, all three bars must be checked together:

Was the prior case discharged? If Chapter 7 discharged, 727(a)(8) controls (8 years Ch7 to Ch7; 1328(f) applies to Ch13 after Ch7 at 4 years). If Chapter 13 discharged, 1328(f)(2) bars another Ch13 discharge for 2 years.

Was the prior case dismissed? Check 109(g)(1) willful-failure ground and 109(g)(2) MFRS-voluntary-dismissal ground. Check the dismissal order for any "with prejudice" language.

Was there a sanctions order in the prior case? Some New Hampshire judges enter injunctions against refiling under 105(a) as part of sanctions, independent of 109(g) and 349.

Run our refile-timing calculator to see your earliest allowable refile date.

New Hampshire Chapter 20 Strategy

"Chapter 20" is the informal name for filing Chapter 7 to discharge unsecured debt, then filing Chapter 13 immediately after to restructure a mortgage, vehicle loan, or priority tax debt even though 1328(f) bars a second discharge.

In a New Hampshire Chapter 20, the second-case Chapter 13 plan:

Cures mortgage arrears under 1322(b)(5) over the plan term.

Strips wholly-unsecured junior mortgages where state valuation supports it.

Pays priority taxes and secured vehicle loans through the plan.

Does not result in a discharge at completion - but reorganization still proceeds.

For New Hampshire's high-dismissal chapter 13 environment, the Chapter 20 path often works better than a single Chapter 13 when substantial unsecured debt exists.

Corporate and Small-Business Refile Constraints

Note: entity debtors (LLCs, corporations) generally cannot file pro se - they must be represented by counsel to handle plan-level matters. This is a practical constraint on any refile strategy where the debtor is a business entity rather than an individual.

See corporate refile rules for the Sub V reorganization refile and the rules on pre-confirmation versus post-confirmation filings.

109(g) 180-day bar

See the 727(a)(8) eight-year rule for the full mechanics.

Section 1328(f): The 4-Year Chapter 13-After-Chapter 7 Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 1328(f)(1), a Chapter 13 debtor cannot receive a discharge if a Chapter 7, 11, or 12 discharge was entered in a case filed within 4 years before the current filing.

This is the so-called "Chapter 20" strategy: filing Chapter 7 first for unsecured-debt discharge, then Chapter 13 to cram down or cure secured debt. The Chapter 13 can still be filed before the 4 years, but without a discharge at completion.

Section 1328(f)(2) adds a 2-year bar on Chapter 13 after a prior Chapter 13 discharge.

4 years is from filing date of prior case to filing date of new case, not discharge date.

For North Carolina filers considering the Chapter 20 route, the 4-year bar is a planning constraint, not an absolute stopper - many debtors file the second case intentionally knowing a no-discharge plan still works.

See the 1328(f) four-year rule for a worked example.

Section 109(g): The 180-Day Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 109(g), a debtor cannot be a debtor in any chapter for 180 days after a prior case is dismissed if either:

109(g)(1) - the case was dismissed for "willful failure" to abide by court orders or to appear in proper prosecution of the case; or

109(g)(2) - the debtor voluntarily dismissed the case after a creditor filed a motion for relief from the automatic stay (MFRS).

NC chapter 13 dismissal rates are mid-range.

109(g)(2) is the most common trap for North Carolina vehicle-loan and mortgage debtors: after a creditor files MFRS, if the debtor voluntarily dismisses to avoid an adverse ruling, the 180-day bar kicks in automatically - no court order needed.

See 109(g) dismissal bar.

Dismissal With Prejudice in North Carolina

Separate from the statutory 180 days, North Carolina bankruptcy courts can dismiss a case "with prejudice" under 11 U.S.C. Section 349(a) and bar refiling for a longer period - commonly 1 year, 2 years, or (rarely) permanently.

Typical triggers in North Carolina practice:

Serial filings designed to stop foreclosure without any plan of reorganization.

Failure to make plan payments repeatedly across multiple cases.

Bad-faith filings where the petition was not accompanied by schedules or where schedules contained materially false statements.

Dismissal with prejudice orders bind the debtor under res judicata and must be vacated (via Rule 60(b)) before any refile.

North Carolina Federal Bankruptcy Data

Refile timing in North Carolina depends on both the federal statute and the local dismissal/relief-from-stay practices reflected in the case data.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 827 consumer bankruptcy cases from North Carolina's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 7273n/an/a

Chapter 13554n/an/a

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Stacking the Three Bars in North Carolina

For a North Carolina filer considering a second case, all three bars must be checked together:

Was the prior case discharged? If Chapter 7 discharged, 727(a)(8) controls (8 years Ch7 to Ch7; 1328(f) applies to Ch13 after Ch7 at 4 years). If Chapter 13 discharged, 1328(f)(2) bars another Ch13 discharge for 2 years.

Was the prior case dismissed? Check 109(g)(1) willful-failure ground and 109(g)(2) MFRS-voluntary-dismissal ground. Check the dismissal order for any "with prejudice" language.

Was there a sanctions order in the prior case? Some North Carolina judges enter injunctions against refiling under 105(a) as part of sanctions, independent of 109(g) and 349.

Run our refile-timing calculator to see your earliest allowable refile date.

North Carolina Chapter 20 Strategy

"Chapter 20" is the informal name for filing Chapter 7 to discharge unsecured debt, then filing Chapter 13 immediately after to restructure a mortgage, vehicle loan, or priority tax debt even though 1328(f) bars a second discharge.

In a North Carolina Chapter 20, the second-case Chapter 13 plan:

Cures mortgage arrears under 1322(b)(5) over the plan term.

Strips wholly-unsecured junior mortgages where state valuation supports it.

Pays priority taxes and secured vehicle loans through the plan.

Does not result in a discharge at completion - but reorganization still proceeds.

For North Carolina's high-dismissal chapter 13 environment, the Chapter 20 path often works better than a single Chapter 13 when substantial unsecured debt exists.

Corporate and Small-Business Refile Constraints

Note: entity debtors (LLCs, corporations) generally cannot file pro se - they must be represented by counsel to handle plan-level matters. This is a practical constraint on any refile strategy where the debtor is a business entity rather than an individual.

See corporate refile rules for the Sub V reorganization refile and the rules on pre-confirmation versus post-confirmation filings.

109(g) 180-day bar

## Can I File Bankruptcy Again in North Dakota? [2026] Refile Timing Rules
Source: https://canifileagain.org/states/north-dakota.html

← canifileagain.org home

Can I File Bankruptcy Again in North Dakota? [2026] Refile Timing Rules

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for North Dakota residents.

Can You File Bankruptcy Again in North Dakota?

Yes - but the timing depends on three separate federal statutes and the reason your prior case ended. This page walks through each bar for North Dakota filers.

Section 727(a)(8) - 8-year bar on a second Chapter 7 discharge after a prior Chapter 7 discharge.

Section 1328(f) - 4-year bar on a Chapter 13 discharge when the prior case was a Chapter 7/11/12 discharge (measured from the filing date of the prior case, not the discharge date).

Section 109(g) - 180-day bar on any new filing when the prior case was dismissed for willful failure to abide by court orders or was voluntarily dismissed after a motion for relief from stay.

North Dakota bankruptcy court applies 8th Circuit 109(g) standards. Low volume.

Section 727(a)(8): The 8-Year Chapter 7-After-Chapter 7 Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 727(a)(8), a Chapter 7 debtor cannot receive a second Chapter 7 discharge within 8 years of filing the prior case that produced a discharge.

The 8 years runs from filing date to filing date, not discharge to filing.

If the prior case was dismissed rather than discharged, 727(a)(8) does not bar the refile - but 109(g) might.

A North Dakota filer whose prior Chapter 7 was filed January 1, 2018, can file a new Chapter 7 on or after January 1, 2026.

See the 727(a)(8) eight-year rule for the full mechanics.

Section 1328(f): The 4-Year Chapter 13-After-Chapter 7 Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 1328(f)(1), a Chapter 13 debtor cannot receive a discharge if a Chapter 7, 11, or 12 discharge was entered in a case filed within 4 years before the current filing.

This is the so-called "Chapter 20" strategy: filing Chapter 7 first for unsecured-debt discharge, then Chapter 13 to cram down or cure secured debt. The Chapter 13 can still be filed before the 4 years, but without a discharge at completion.

Section 1328(f)(2) adds a 2-year bar on Chapter 13 after a prior Chapter 13 discharge.

4 years is from filing date of prior case to filing date of new case, not discharge date.

For North Dakota filers considering the Chapter 20 route, the 4-year bar is a planning constraint, not an absolute stopper - many debtors file the second case intentionally knowing a no-discharge plan still works.

See the 1328(f) four-year rule for a worked example.

Section 109(g): The 180-Day Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 109(g), a debtor cannot be a debtor in any chapter for 180 days after a prior case is dismissed if either:

109(g)(2) - the debtor voluntarily dismissed the case after a creditor filed a motion for relief from the automatic stay (MFRS).

ND has one federal bankruptcy district.

109(g)(2) is the most common trap for North Dakota vehicle-loan and mortgage debtors: after a creditor files MFRS, if the debtor voluntarily dismisses to avoid an adverse ruling, the 180-day bar kicks in automatically - no court order needed.

See 109(g) dismissal bar.

Serial filings designed to stop foreclosure without any plan of reorganization.

Failure to make plan payments repeatedly across multiple cases.

Bad-faith filings where the petition was not accompanied by schedules or where schedules contained materially false statements.

Dismissal with prejudice orders bind the debtor under res judicata and must be vacated (via Rule 60(b)) before any refile.

For a North Dakota filer considering a second case, all three bars must be checked together:

Was the prior case discharged? If Chapter 7 discharged, 727(a)(8) controls (8 years Ch7 to Ch7; 1328(f) applies to Ch13 after Ch7 at 4 years). If Chapter 13 discharged, 1328(f)(2) bars another Ch13 discharge for 2 years.

Was there a sanctions order in the prior case? Some North Dakota judges enter injunctions against refiling under 105(a) as part of sanctions, independent of 109(g) and 349.

Oregon Chapter 20 Strategy

"Chapter 20" is the informal name for filing Chapter 7 to discharge unsecured debt, then filing Chapter 13 immediately after to restructure a mortgage, vehicle loan, or priority tax debt even though 1328(f) bars a second discharge.

In a Oregon Chapter 20, the second-case Chapter 13 plan:

Cures mortgage arrears under 1322(b)(5) over the plan term.

Strips wholly-unsecured junior mortgages where state valuation supports it.

Pays priority taxes and secured vehicle loans through the plan.

Does not result in a discharge at completion - but reorganization still proceeds.

For Oregon's high-dismissal chapter 13 environment, the Chapter 20 path often works better than a single Chapter 13 when substantial unsecured debt exists.

Corporate and Small-Business Refile Constraints

Note: entity debtors (LLCs, corporations) generally cannot file pro se - they must be represented by counsel to handle plan-level matters. This is a practical constraint on any refile strategy where the debtor is a business entity rather than an individual.

See corporate refile rules for the Sub V reorganization refile and the rules on pre-confirmation versus post-confirmation filings.

## Can I File Bankruptcy Again in Pennsylvania? [2026] Refile Timing Rules
Source: https://canifileagain.org/states/pennsylvania.html

← canifileagain.org home

Can I File Bankruptcy Again in Pennsylvania? [2026] Refile Timing Rules

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Pennsylvania residents.

Can You File Bankruptcy Again in Pennsylvania?

Yes - but the timing depends on three separate federal statutes and the reason your prior case ended. This page walks through each bar for Pennsylvania filers.

Section 727(a)(8) - 8-year bar on a second Chapter 7 discharge after a prior Chapter 7 discharge.

Section 1328(f) - 4-year bar on a Chapter 13 discharge when the prior case was a Chapter 7/11/12 discharge (measured from the filing date of the prior case, not the discharge date).

Section 109(g) - 180-day bar on any new filing when the prior case was dismissed for willful failure to abide by court orders or was voluntarily dismissed after a motion for relief from stay.

Pennsylvania bankruptcy courts (Eastern, Middle, Western) apply 3rd Circuit 109(g) standards. Philadelphia (E.D. Pa.) and Pittsburgh (W.D. Pa.) handle most consumer cases.

Section 727(a)(8): The 8-Year Chapter 7-After-Chapter 7 Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 727(a)(8), a Chapter 7 debtor cannot receive a second Chapter 7 discharge within 8 years of filing the prior case that produced a discharge.

The 8 years runs from filing date to filing date, not discharge to filing.

If the prior case was dismissed rather than discharged, 727(a)(8) does not bar the refile - but 109(g) might.

A Pennsylvania filer whose prior Chapter 7 was filed January 1, 2018, can file a new Chapter 7 on or after January 1, 2026.

See the 727(a)(8) eight-year rule for the full mechanics.

Section 1328(f): The 4-Year Chapter 13-After-Chapter 7 Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 1328(f)(1), a Chapter 13 debtor cannot receive a discharge if a Chapter 7, 11, or 12 discharge was entered in a case filed within 4 years before the current filing.

This is the so-called "Chapter 20" strategy: filing Chapter 7 first for unsecured-debt discharge, then Chapter 13 to cram down or cure secured debt. The Chapter 13 can still be filed before the 4 years, but without a discharge at completion.

Section 1328(f)(2) adds a 2-year bar on Chapter 13 after a prior Chapter 13 discharge.

4 years is from filing date of prior case to filing date of new case, not discharge date.

For Pennsylvania filers considering the Chapter 20 route, the 4-year bar is a planning constraint, not an absolute stopper - many debtors file the second case intentionally knowing a no-discharge plan still works.

See the 1328(f) four-year rule for a worked example.

Section 109(g): The 180-Day Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 109(g), a debtor cannot be a debtor in any chapter for 180 days after a prior case is dismissed if either:

109(g)(1) - the case was dismissed for "willful failure" to abide by court orders or to appear in proper prosecution of the case; or

109(g)(2) - the debtor voluntarily dismissed the case after a creditor filed a motion for relief from the automatic stay (MFRS).

PA chapter 13 dismissal rates moderate.

109(g)(2) is the most common trap for Pennsylvania vehicle-loan and mortgage debtors: after a creditor files MFRS, if the debtor voluntarily dismisses to avoid an adverse ruling, the 180-day bar kicks in automatically - no court order needed.

See 109(g) dismissal bar.

Dismissal With Prejudice in Pennsylvania

Separate from the statutory 180 days, Pennsylvania bankruptcy courts can dismiss a case "with prejudice" under 11 U.S.C. Section 349(a) and bar refiling for a longer period - commonly 1 year, 2 years, or (rarely) permanently.

Typical triggers in Pennsylvania practice:

Serial filings designed to stop foreclosure without any plan of reorganization.

Failure to make plan payments repeatedly across multiple cases.

Bad-faith filings where the petition was not accompanied by schedules or where schedules contained materially false statements.

Dismissal with prejudice orders bind the debtor under res judicata and must be vacated (via Rule 60(b)) before any refile.

Pennsylvania Federal Bankruptcy Data

Refile timing in Pennsylvania depends on both the federal statute and the local dismissal/relief-from-stay practices reflected in the case data.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,513 consumer bankruptcy cases from Pennsylvania's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 7415n/an/a

Chapter 131,098n/an/a

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Stacking the Three Bars in Pennsylvania

For a Pennsylvania filer considering a second case, all three bars must be checked together:

Was the prior case discharged? If Chapter 7 discharged, 727(a)(8) controls (8 years Ch7 to Ch7; 1328(f) applies to Ch13 after Ch7 at 4 years). If Chapter 13 discharged, 1328(f)(2) bars another Ch13 discharge for 2 years.

Was the prior case dismissed? Check 109(g)(1) willful-failure ground and 109(g)(2) MFRS-voluntary-dismissal ground. Check the dismissal order for any "with prejudice" language.

Was there a sanctions order in the prior case? Some Pennsylvania judges enter injunctions against refiling under 105(a) as part of sanctions, independent of 109(g) and 349.

Run our refile-timing calculator to see your earliest allowable refile date.

Pennsylvania Chapter 20 Strategy

"Chapter 20" is the informal name for filing Chapter 7 to discharge unsecured debt, then filing Chapter 13 immediately after to restructure a mortgage, vehicle loan, or priority tax debt even though 1328(f) bars a second discharge.

In a Pennsylvania Chapter 20, the second-case Chapter 13 plan:

Cures mortgage arrears under 1322(b)(5) over the plan term.

Strips wholly-unsecured junior mortgages where state valuation supports it.

Pays priority taxes and secured vehicle loans through the plan.

Does not result in a discharge at completion - but reorganization still proceeds.

For Pennsylvania's high-dismissal chapter 13 environment, the Chapter 20 path often works better than a single Chapter 13 when substantial unsecured debt exists.

Corporate and Small-Business Refile Constraints

Note: entity debtors (LLCs, corporations) generally cannot file pro se - they must be represented by counsel to handle plan-level matters. This is a practical constraint on any refile strategy where the debtor is a business entity rather than an individual.

See corporate refile rules for the Sub V reorganization refile and the rules on pre-confirmation versus post-confirmation filings.

Tennessee bankruptcy courts (Eastern, Middle, Western) apply 6th Circuit 109(g) standards. Memphis (W.D. Tenn.) and Nashville (M.D. Tenn.) have high chapter 13 volume.

Section 727(a)(8): The 8-Year Chapter 7-After-Chapter 7 Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 727(a)(8), a Chapter 7 debtor cannot receive a second Chapter 7 discharge within 8 years of filing the prior case that produced a discharge.

The 8 years runs from filing date to filing date, not discharge to filing.

If the prior case was dismissed rather than discharged, 727(a)(8) does not bar the refile - but 109(g) might.

A Tennessee filer whose prior Chapter 7 was filed January 1, 2018, can file a new Chapter 7 on or after January 1, 2026.

See the 727(a)(8) eight-year rule for the full mechanics.

Section 1328(f): The 4-Year Chapter 13-After-Chapter 7 Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 1328(f)(1), a Chapter 13 debtor cannot receive a discharge if a Chapter 7, 11, or 12 discharge was entered in a case filed within 4 years before the current filing.

This is the so-called "Chapter 20" strategy: filing Chapter 7 first for unsecured-debt discharge, then Chapter 13 to cram down or cure secured debt. The Chapter 13 can still be filed before the 4 years, but without a discharge at completion.

Section 1328(f)(2) adds a 2-year bar on Chapter 13 after a prior Chapter 13 discharge.

4 years is from filing date of prior case to filing date of new case, not discharge date.

For Tennessee filers considering the Chapter 20 route, the 4-year bar is a planning constraint, not an absolute stopper - many debtors file the second case intentionally knowing a no-discharge plan still works.

See the 1328(f) four-year rule for a worked example.

Section 109(g): The 180-Day Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 109(g), a debtor cannot be a debtor in any chapter for 180 days after a prior case is dismissed if either:

109(g)(1) - the case was dismissed for "willful failure" to abide by court orders or to appear in proper prosecution of the case; or

109(g)(2) - the debtor voluntarily dismissed the case after a creditor filed a motion for relief from the automatic stay (MFRS).

TN chapter 13 dismissal rates are high; 109(g) highly active.

109(g)(2) is the most common trap for Tennessee vehicle-loan and mortgage debtors: after a creditor files MFRS, if the debtor voluntarily dismisses to avoid an adverse ruling, the 180-day bar kicks in automatically - no court order needed.

See 109(g) dismissal bar.

Dismissal With Prejudice in Tennessee

Separate from the statutory 180 days, Tennessee bankruptcy courts can dismiss a case "with prejudice" under 11 U.S.C. Section 349(a) and bar refiling for a longer period - commonly 1 year, 2 years, or (rarely) permanently.

Typical triggers in Tennessee practice:

Serial filings designed to stop foreclosure without any plan of reorganization.

Failure to make plan payments repeatedly across multiple cases.

Bad-faith filings where the petition was not accompanied by schedules or where schedules contained materially false statements.

Dismissal with prejudice orders bind the debtor under res judicata and must be vacated (via Rule 60(b)) before any refile.

Tennessee Federal Bankruptcy Data

Refile timing in Tennessee depends on both the federal statute and the local dismissal/relief-from-stay practices reflected in the case data.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,840 consumer bankruptcy cases from Tennessee's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 758995.5%4.5%

Chapter 131,25117.3%82.7%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Stacking the Three Bars in Tennessee

For a Tennessee filer considering a second case, all three bars must be checked together:

Was the prior case discharged? If Chapter 7 discharged, 727(a)(8) controls (8 years Ch7 to Ch7; 1328(f) applies to Ch13 after Ch7 at 4 years). If Chapter 13 discharged, 1328(f)(2) bars another Ch13 discharge for 2 years.

Was the prior case dismissed? Check 109(g)(1) willful-failure ground and 109(g)(2) MFRS-voluntary-dismissal ground. Check the dismissal order for any "with prejudice" language.

Was there a sanctions order in the prior case? Some Tennessee judges enter injunctions against refiling under 105(a) as part of sanctions, independent of 109(g) and 349.

Run our refile-timing calculator to see your earliest allowable refile date.

Tennessee Chapter 20 Strategy

"Chapter 20" is the informal name for filing Chapter 7 to discharge unsecured debt, then filing Chapter 13 immediately after to restructure a mortgage, vehicle loan, or priority tax debt even though 1328(f) bars a second discharge.

In a Tennessee Chapter 20, the second-case Chapter 13 plan:

Cures mortgage arrears under 1322(b)(5) over the plan term.

Strips wholly-unsecured junior mortgages where state valuation supports it.

Pays priority taxes and secured vehicle loans through the plan.

Does not result in a discharge at completion - but reorganization still proceeds.

For Tennessee's high-dismissal chapter 13 environment, the Chapter 20 path often works better than a single Chapter 13 when substantial unsecured debt exists.

Corporate and Small-Business Refile Constraints

Note: entity debtors (LLCs, corporations) generally cannot file pro se - they must be represented by counsel to handle plan-level matters. This is a practical constraint on any refile strategy where the debtor is a business entity rather than an individual.

See corporate refile rules for the Sub V reorganization refile and the rules on pre-confirmation versus post-confirmation filings.

109(g) 180-day bar

## Can I File Bankruptcy Again in Texas? [2026] Refile Timing Rules

Can I File Bankruptcy Again in Texas? [2026] Refile Timing Rules

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Texas residents.

Can You File Bankruptcy Again in Texas?

Yes - but the timing depends on three separate federal statutes and the reason your prior case ended. This page walks through each bar for Texas filers.

Section 727(a)(8) - 8-year bar on a second Chapter 7 discharge after a prior Chapter 7 discharge.

Section 1328(f) - 4-year bar on a Chapter 13 discharge when the prior case was a Chapter 7/11/12 discharge (measured from the filing date of the prior case, not the discharge date).

Section 109(g) - 180-day bar on any new filing when the prior case was dismissed for willful failure to abide by court orders or was voluntarily dismissed after a motion for relief from stay.

Texas bankruptcy courts (Northern, Eastern, Southern, Western) apply 5th Circuit 109(g) standards. S.D. Tex. (Houston) is high-volume for both consumer and business.

Stacking the Three Bars in Virginia

For a Virginia filer considering a second case, all three bars must be checked together:

Was the prior case discharged? If Chapter 7 discharged, 727(a)(8) controls (8 years Ch7 to Ch7; 1328(f) applies to Ch13 after Ch7 at 4 years). If Chapter 13 discharged, 1328(f)(2) bars another Ch13 discharge for 2 years.

Was the prior case dismissed? Check 109(g)(1) willful-failure ground and 109(g)(2) MFRS-voluntary-dismissal ground. Check the dismissal order for any "with prejudice" language.

Was there a sanctions order in the prior case? Some Virginia judges enter injunctions against refiling under 105(a) as part of sanctions, independent of 109(g) and 349.

Run our refile-timing calculator to see your earliest allowable refile date.

Virginia Chapter 20 Strategy

"Chapter 20" is the informal name for filing Chapter 7 to discharge unsecured debt, then filing Chapter 13 immediately after to restructure a mortgage, vehicle loan, or priority tax debt even though 1328(f) bars a second discharge.

In a Virginia Chapter 20, the second-case Chapter 13 plan:

Cures mortgage arrears under 1322(b)(5) over the plan term.

Strips wholly-unsecured junior mortgages where state valuation supports it.

Pays priority taxes and secured vehicle loans through the plan.

Does not result in a discharge at completion - but reorganization still proceeds.

For Virginia's high-dismissal chapter 13 environment, the Chapter 20 path often works better than a single Chapter 13 when substantial unsecured debt exists.

Corporate and Small-Business Refile Constraints

Note: entity debtors (LLCs, corporations) generally cannot file pro se - they must be represented by counsel to handle plan-level matters. This is a practical constraint on any refile strategy where the debtor is a business entity rather than an individual.

See corporate refile rules for the Sub V reorganization refile and the rules on pre-confirmation versus post-confirmation filings.

## Can I File Bankruptcy Again in Washington? [2026] Refile Timing Rules
Source: https://canifileagain.org/states/washington.html

← canifileagain.org home

Can I File Bankruptcy Again in Washington? [2026] Refile Timing Rules

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Washington residents.

Can You File Bankruptcy Again in Washington?

Yes - but the timing depends on three separate federal statutes and the reason your prior case ended. This page walks through each bar for Washington filers.

Section 727(a)(8) - 8-year bar on a second Chapter 7 discharge after a prior Chapter 7 discharge.

Section 1328(f) - 4-year bar on a Chapter 13 discharge when the prior case was a Chapter 7/11/12 discharge (measured from the filing date of the prior case, not the discharge date).

Section 109(g) - 180-day bar on any new filing when the prior case was dismissed for willful failure to abide by court orders or was voluntarily dismissed after a motion for relief from stay.

Washington bankruptcy courts (Eastern, Western) apply 9th Circuit 109(g) standards.

Section 727(a)(8): The 8-Year Chapter 7-After-Chapter 7 Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 727(a)(8), a Chapter 7 debtor cannot receive a second Chapter 7 discharge within 8 years of filing the prior case that produced a discharge.

The 8 years runs from filing date to filing date, not discharge to filing.

If the prior case was dismissed rather than discharged, 727(a)(8) does not bar the refile - but 109(g) might.

A Washington filer whose prior Chapter 7 was filed January 1, 2018, can file a new Chapter 7 on or after January 1, 2026.

See the 727(a)(8) eight-year rule for the full mechanics.

Section 1328(f): The 4-Year Chapter 13-After-Chapter 7 Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 1328(f)(1), a Chapter 13 debtor cannot receive a discharge if a Chapter 7, 11, or 12 discharge was entered in a case filed within 4 years before the current filing.

This is the so-called "Chapter 20" strategy: filing Chapter 7 first for unsecured-debt discharge, then Chapter 13 to cram down or cure secured debt. The Chapter 13 can still be filed before the 4 years, but without a discharge at completion.

Section 1328(f)(2) adds a 2-year bar on Chapter 13 after a prior Chapter 13 discharge.

4 years is from filing date of prior case to filing date of new case, not discharge date.

For Washington filers considering the Chapter 20 route, the 4-year bar is a planning constraint, not an absolute stopper - many debtors file the second case intentionally knowing a no-discharge plan still works.

See the 1328(f) four-year rule for a worked example.

Section 109(g): The 180-Day Bar

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 109(g), a debtor cannot be a debtor in any chapter for 180 days after a prior case is dismissed if either:

109(g)(1) - the case was dismissed for "willful failure" to abide by court orders or to appear in proper prosecution of the case; or

109(g)(2) - the debtor voluntarily dismissed the case after a creditor filed a motion for relief from the automatic stay (MFRS).

WA chapter 7 discharge rates are among the nation's highest.

109(g)(2) is the most common trap for Washington vehicle-loan and mortgage debtors: after a creditor files MFRS, if the debtor voluntarily dismisses to avoid an adverse ruling, the 180-day bar kicks in automatically - no court order needed.

See 109(g) dismissal bar.

Dismissal With Prejudice in Washington

Separate from the statutory 180 days, Washington bankruptcy courts can dismiss a case "with prejudice" under 11 U.S.C. Section 349(a) and bar refiling for a longer period - commonly 1 year, 2 years, or (rarely) permanently.

Typical triggers in Washington practice:

Serial filings designed to stop foreclosure without any plan of reorganization.

Failure to make plan payments repeatedly across multiple cases.

Bad-faith filings where the petition was not accompanied by schedules or where schedules contained materially false statements.

Dismissal with prejudice orders bind the debtor under res judicata and must be vacated (via Rule 60(b)) before any refile.

Stacking the Three Bars in Washington

For a Washington filer considering a second case, all three bars must be checked together:

Was the prior case discharged? If Chapter 7 discharged, 727(a)(8) controls (8 years Ch7 to Ch7; 1328(f) applies to Ch13 after Ch7 at 4 years). If Chapter 13 discharged, 1328(f)(2) bars another Ch13 discharge for 2 years.

Was the prior case dismissed? Check 109(g)(1) willful-failure ground and 109(g)(2) MFRS-voluntary-dismissal ground. Check the dismissal order for any "with prejudice" language.

Was there a sanctions order in the prior case? Some Washington judges enter injunctions against refiling under 105(a) as part of sanctions, independent of 109(g) and 349.

Run our refile-timing calculator to see your earliest allowable refile date.

Washington Chapter 20 Strategy

"Chapter 20" is the informal name for filing Chapter 7 to discharge unsecured debt, then filing Chapter 13 immediately after to restructure a mortgage, vehicle loan, or priority tax debt even though 1328(f) bars a second discharge.

In a Washington Chapter 20, the second-case Chapter 13 plan:

Cures mortgage arrears under 1322(b)(5) over the plan term.

Strips wholly-unsecured junior mortgages where state valuation supports it.

Pays priority taxes and secured vehicle loans through the plan.

Does not result in a discharge at completion - but reorganization still proceeds.

For Washington's high-dismissal chapter 13 environment, the Chapter 20 path often works better than a single Chapter 13 when substantial unsecured debt exists.

Corporate and Small-Business Refile Constraints

Note: entity debtors (LLCs, corporations) generally cannot file pro se - they must be represented by counsel to handle plan-level matters. This is a practical constraint on any refile strategy where the debtor is a business entity rather than an individual.

See corporate refile rules for the Sub V reorganization refile and the rules on pre-confirmation versus post-confirmation filings.
